claims.text: A physics-informed machine-learning model can combine ab initio-derived inputs with experimental measurements for property prediction.
Including defect and oxygen-impurity scattering descriptors will make conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurate than predictions from traditional perfect-crystal analytical models.
The proposed model uses local defect densities, oxygen-impurity scattering strengths, and temperature-dependent activation energies obtained from ab initio calculations.
Quantum effects and defect-induced scattering dominate or are prominent in HfNbTaTiZr at 0–200 K.
Thermal activation coexists with oxygen-impurity scattering in HfNbTaTiZr at 300–1200 K.
Conductivity measurements are available for HfNbTaTiZr in the stated temperature regimes, including measurements on a specimen containing about 1 wt.% oxygen.
Defects in real samples act as electron-scattering centers.
Oxygen impurities in HfNbTaTiZr act as electron-scattering centers.
Defects and oxygen impurities perturb the alloy's local electronic structure and conductivity.
Accounting for point-defect and oxygen-impurity scattering changes the predicted electron-scattering rates.
At low temperature, increased defect scattering reduces conductivity relative to ideal-crystal predictions.
At high temperature, oxygen modifies thermally activated conduction channels and produces distinct conduction behavior.
Perfect-crystal analytical models typically overestimate the conductivity of realistic HfNbTaTiZr.
Existing defect-free analytical models show sizeable discrepancies from conductivity measurements on HfNbTaTiZr containing about 1 wt.% oxygen.
Machine-learning approaches can achieve greater predictive accuracy than some phenomenological approaches for high-entropy-alloy problems.

claims.text: The proposed model will predict held-out conductivity at 150 K or 1000 K with less than 10% relative error.
The model's claimed applicability is limited to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K and to oxygen and defect concentrations similar to those of the approximately 1 wt.% oxygen specimen.
A held-out relative error greater than 10% at the benchmark temperatures is defined as falsifying the model's claimed meaningful improvement.
